questions.question: What is the core job of a circuit breaker?
options: Repair the failed dependency
Stop repeated calls that are unlikely to succeed and control recovery probes
Guarantee every fallback is correct
Replace all per-attempt timeouts
questions.explanation: A breaker contains repeated failure at the caller. Dependency repair, timeout policy, and fallback correctness remain separate responsibilities.

questions.question: A window contains 30 calls, all of which fail, but the policy requires at least 100 calls. What should the breaker do?
options: Open because the measured failure rate is 100%
Close permanently
Keep measuring because the sample has not reached the evidence minimum
Send 70 synthetic failures
questions.explanation: A minimum call count protects low-volume paths from unstable decisions based on tiny samples, even when the computed rate is alarming.

questions.question: Why can slow successful calls open a circuit?
options: They always return invalid data
They can hold caller threads, connections, and latency budget until the system cascades
They prove the network is disconnected
They eliminate the need for a bulkhead
questions.explanation: A dependency can eventually succeed while consuming scarce caller capacity. A separate slow-call boundary detects that brownout.

questions.question: What does expiration of the open wait prove?
options: The dependency is healthy
The fallback is fresh
A limited recovery probe may now be attempted
All traffic can be restored immediately
questions.explanation: Time passing is only permission to gather new evidence. Half-open probes determine whether recovery satisfies the declared contract.

questions.question: A half-open cohort has acceptable p95 latency but 30% of probes fail against a 10% maximum. What is the correct transition?
options: Close because latency passed
Stay half-open forever
Return to open because one recovery boundary failed
Disable failure classification
questions.explanation: Recovery requires every declared boundary to pass. Restoring full traffic after a failed probe contract can overload a partially recovered dependency.

questions.question: Why should independent shards or regions usually have separate breakers?
options: One global breaker can block healthy paths because an unrelated failure is aggregated into it
Separate breakers make every operation idempotent
A breaker must run inside the dependency
Regions never share failure modes
questions.explanation: Breaker scope should match the failure domain. Aggregating independent resources can turn a local failure into unnecessary global rejection.

questions.question: Which fallback is unsafe without additional product semantics?
options: Hide a noncritical recommendations panel
Return an explicit service-unavailable response
Report a payment as accepted when authorization never completed
Show a labeled last-known-good catalog entry
questions.explanation: Failing fast does not permit fabricated success. A fallback must preserve the correctness contract of the operation or expose the degradation explicitly.

questions.question: Why is retrying at two layers with three attempts each dangerous?
options: It can multiply into nine dependency attempts and amplify an outage
It forces the breaker to remain closed
It removes all jitter
It guarantees duplicate state transitions
questions.explanation: Layered retries multiply work. Central ownership, finite attempts, backoff, jitter, and an aggregate retry budget are needed to avoid a retry storm.
